newsitem.title: USA: Tepid U.S. incomes hint at modest Q3 strength.
newsitem.headline: Tepid U.S. incomes hint at modest Q3 strength.

text.p: Reduced wages did less damage to paychecks in July than expected, but economists said the slight rise in July personal income was not a convincing sign of economic strength.
Personal income rose 0.1 percent in July versus a 0.9 percent rise in June. Estimates called for a 0.1 percent fall.
"I think the (incomes) number was a little stronger than anticipated but it is still a weak number," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.

"In fact, if you look at the consumer spending numbers and the downward revision in June, it looks like the third quarter is off to a very weak start, in terms of how these numbers translate into the Gross Domestic Product statistics," she added.
As expected, July personal spending increased by 0.2 percent but consumption in June was revised downward to a 0.4 percent fall from a previous 0.2 percent decline.
On Thursday, U.S. bonds and stocks were jolted after second quarter GDP was revised to a robust 4.8 percent rate of growth from an already steamy 4.2 percent rate.
The GDP revision alarmed the markets which until recently had been expecting the economy to come off its boil, enabling the Federal Reserve to hold off on credit tightening.

But while the personal income numbers were near expectations, economists had expected a curtailed workweek, as reflected in the Labor Department's July employment data, to take a bigger bite out of pay.
Hourly earnings fell 0.2 percent in July to an average of $11.00, according to the Labor survey. The average workweek shortened to 34.3 hours in July from 34.7 hours in June.
"We had a drop in hours and that is why wages and salaries (in the employment data) were off," said Cynthia Latta, senior financial economist at DRI/McGraw Hill.
"There are really no surprises here. It looks weak but when you know what's behind the numbers, it is not all that weak."

Sally Kleinman, senior domestic economist at Chase Securities Inc, added: "It was pretty much as expected. It's just helping people focus on the fact second quarter growth was so strong and we started the third quarter on a very poor footing." -- 212-859-1667
